best-hay-for-rabbits.title: Hay we'd reach for
best-hay-for-rabbits.intro: Good hay should smell sweet, look green and feel soft rather than dusty. These are reliable places to start.

picks.why: High in fibre and low in calcium, so it suits most adult rabbits as their main hay.
Softer and sweeter-smelling than timothy, which can tempt rabbits that pick at their hay.
A mix of grasses with different textures, and far cheaper per kilo for homes with more than one rabbit.
Keeps hay off the floor and away from the litter area, so more of it gets eaten instead of trampled.

best-bedding-for-rabbits.title: Bedding we'd reach for
best-bedding-for-rabbits.intro: Safe if nibbled, absorbent and low in dust. Avoid cedar, untreated pine, clay cat litter and anything scented.

picks.why: Soft, absorbent, low-dust recycled paper that's safe if your rabbit nibbles it.
Compressed paper pellets soak up urine well and keep the tray easy to clean.
Aspen doesn't contain the aromatic oils found in pine and cedar, so it's a safer wood choice.
Popular for indoor setups: moisture wicks through to the absorbent layer underneath, and they go in the wash.

rabbit-toys.title: Toys we'd reach for
rabbit-toys.intro: Look for untreated, natural materials with no small parts that could be swallowed.

picks.why: Natural, safe to chew, and fun to toss and roll around.
Untreated fruit wood gives rabbits something worthwhile to gnaw instead of your skirting boards.
Rabbits love a safe tunnel to dash through and hide in, and these are good to nibble too.
Hide pellets or herbs in it to turn feeding time into a sniffing, searching game.
